paragraph.text: N2. "Suffering and death are part of nature"

being part of nature doesn't make something good or indifferent for the one who suffers. Diseases, parasites, famines, natural disasters and death in childbirth also strike human beings through natural causes, and that was never a reason to leave the victims without help. The absence of a culprit matters for judging agents, not for measuring the victims' harm.

this family takes the sentience criterion beyond exploitation. Many vegans disagree with parts of it, and the debate is legitimate. The test proposed in each chapter is simple: apply the same scenario to human beings and see whether the answer would be accepted; if it would not, that shows speciesism.
"That's just how nature is. Some eat others, some get sick, others die. It's part of it."
It only makes sense to speak of moral evil when there's a responsible agent.
In nature, suffering is caused by processes without intention: predation, disease, climate.
So natural suffering isn't a moral evil.
And what isn't a moral evil gives us no reason to act.
P1 and P2 are acceptable if we're talking about blame: a hurricane is guilty of nothing. The problem lies in C2, which jumps from the absence of a culprit to the absence of a victim.
: from "no one is to blame" it doesn't follow that "no one was harmed".
"Nature is cruel, that's how it is."
"Wanting to end suffering in nature is denying life."
"Natural suffering is morally neutral, because it doesn't result from choices."
"It's the circle of life." (which is C6)

Catching a cold is part of life, right? Even so, when you're sick, someone looks after you, gives you medicine and a warm drink. No one says "leave it, it's natural". What's natural can hurt just the same. And when it hurts, we help if we can.

Disease is also part of nature, and we still treat it. You wouldn't leave a child with an infection untreated because bacteria are natural, or refuse to help victims of famine or earthquakes because droughts and earthquakes are natural. That no one is to blame for suffering doesn't make it any less bad for the one who suffers. So the question is whether we can help without causing more harm.
"If a disease is natural, would you stop treating it?"
There being an agent who chose
An arsonist is to blame; lightning isn't
There being a victim who suffered
A forest burned by lightning has as many victims as one burned by an arsonist
For the one who suffers, the origin of the suffering doesn't change what they feel.
Nature has no intentions, but animals have experiences. The suffering of an animal eaten alive by parasites isn't neutral for it.

text.bold: 2. Natural isn't a criterion of good.

paragraph.text: , John Stuart Mill observed that nature does, every day, things for which a human being would be imprisoned or hanged. Copying nature was never a good moral guide (C1).

text.bold: 3. We already intervene in the natural all the time.

paragraph.text: Vaccines, antibiotics, glasses, anaesthesia, shelter from the cold: much of civilization consists of reducing natural suffering.

We don't use this argument for human beings. Diseases, famines caused by droughts and pests, earthquakes, floods and hurricanes are also "part of nature", and we still vaccinate, treat, send food and help the victims. Faced with an epidemic or an earthquake, no one says "it's part of nature, let's not help". The absence of a culprit was never a reason to deny help to humans. Denying it to animals for the same reason is using a criterion we apply only to them.

text.bold: 5. There's no agent, but there's someone who can help.

paragraph.text: Ethics asks not only who caused something, but also what we, who can act, ought to do.

text.bold: 6. Value and morality are different questions.

paragraph.text: Asking whether something is good or bad isn't the same as asking who is responsible for it. We don't conclude that suffering is bad because someone caused it; it's the other way round: we shouldn't cause it because it's bad. A process with no moral agent produces results that are still good or bad for those who live them. The "human touch" changes nothing about the pain (Cunha, 2022, p. 100).

Imagine a factory farm that appeared on its own, with no human behind it: would the reasons to end it be any weaker? Imagine that the plastic that kills turtles formed naturally in the ocean: would it stop being a problem? Finally, imagine a human deliberately designing a system in which each mother produces thousands of young so that almost all of them starve, in which many are eaten alive or consumed by parasites, and in which all of this is hidden behind a beautiful landscape. We'd call that designer a monster. That is the description of nature for most animals (Cunha, 2022, pp. 106–107).

text.bold: 8. "It's part of life" isn't "it should be part of life".

paragraph.text: The environmental philosopher J. Baird Callicott (1980) wrote that refusing suffering and death is refusing the conditions of life. No one denies they are part of life; the question is whether they should remain so when they can be avoided. We also know pain is part of our lives, and we still take painkillers. And "it has always been this way" would prove too much: sexual violence has always existed too (Cunha, 2022, p. 109).

text.bold: 9. "Nature never makes mistakes" assumes a designer.

paragraph.text: It only makes sense to say a process gets things right or wrong if it has goals. Evolutionary biology doesn't attribute goals to natural selection. And even if there were someone behind it, we'd have to show that this someone knows everything and wants what's good for animals, which the daily carnage makes hard to maintain. Nor does it help to say that "everything leads to the best, we just can't see it": by the same reasoning, we shouldn't treat human diseases either (Cunha, 2022, pp. 109–110).

text.bold: 10. Those who find suffering useful prefer, when they can, the benefit without it.

paragraph.text: The environmental philosopher Holmes Rolston III (1992) argues that suffering has value for the animal itself, for other animals and for the species. But most animals in nature suffer from birth to death, with no benefit at all. And when suffering is useful, we prefer to reach the same good without it, as we do when we operate under anesthesia (Cunha, 2022, pp. 103–104).
Nature kills, tortures and destroys all the time; imitating it isn't a moral criterion

The principle being tested is: "suffering that's part of nature doesn't need to be relieved".
We shouldn't treat infections, cancer or malaria
Some people once said so, and lost the debate
Humanitarian aid exists precisely for this
Famine caused by droughts or pests
No one accepts leaving the victims without help

It's right that nature isn't a moral agent and that it makes no sense to blame lions or viruses. It's also right that pain has important biological functions and that tampering with it requires great care.

But the question isn't whether nature is to blame. It's whether we, who can act, have reason to help those who suffer. And the natural origin of suffering has never, in any other context, been a reason not to help.
